A 44-year-old man comes to the office for a routine check-up.  Medical history is significant for hypercholesterolemia, which he has controlled through diet.  His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 56, and his mother, who is still living, has a history of stroke.  Blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min.  Enalapril is prescribed.  During the first 7 days of therapy, the patient's glomerular filtration rate adjusts as shown below.

This response is best explained by an effect of the drug on which of the following renal structures?​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌
explanation:
Angiotensin II is an important blood pressure–regulating hormone that has the following effects:

  • Systemic vasoconstriction
  • Preferential constriction of renal glomerular efferent arterioles (much more than afferent arterioles)
  • Enhancement of adrenal aldosterone secretion

In the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.  ACE inhibitors (eg, enalapril, lisinopril) block this conversion, resulting in reduced angiotensin II activity.  Angiotensin II receptor blockers (eg, losartan) similarly reduce angiotensin II activity but do so via receptor blockade.

Reduced angiotensin II activity alleviates systemic vasoconstriction and decreases aldosterone production to lower systemic blood pressure.  It also slightly decreases glomerular filtration rate (GFR) due to alleviated vasoconstriction of renal glomerular efferent arterioles, which reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and decreases net filtration pressure.

Although the decreased GFR represents reduced kidney function, the reduction is typically mild and mostly temporary.  In patients with RAAS overactivity (eg, hypertension), ongoing ACE inhibition tends to protect the glomerular capillaries and preserve long-term kidney function.

(Choice A)  Prostaglandins induce vasodilation of renal glomerular afferent arterioles; therefore, inhibition of prostaglandins (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) can reduce renal blood flow and decrease GFR.  Angiotensin II does not have much effect on afferent arterioles; therefore, inhibition of angiotensin II does not either.

(Choices B, D, and E)  The distal tubules, proximal tubules, and vasa recta are not substantially affected by angiotensin II or its inhibition.

Educational objective:Angiotensin II preferentially constricts renal glomerular efferent arterioles, which helps maintain glomerular filtration rate (GFR).  ACE inhibitors (eg, enalapril, lisinopril) reduce angiotensin II activity, which alleviates vasoconstriction of efferent arterioles and commonly causes a slight decrease in GFR.​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌
